paper_title: When Does Reasoning Help Entity Disambiguation? Small LLMs In-Domain and Under Shift

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Entity disambiguation (mapping ambiguous mentions in text to entities in a knowledge base) is a foundational step in tasks such as knowledge graph construction, question answering, and information extraction. Recent work has applied LLMs to this problem, achieving stateof-the-art performance. Notably, reasoning LLMs have been shown to perform entity disambiguation in a true zero-shot fashion, generalizing across knowledge bases and domains. However, it is unclear whether this capability survives, or remains competitive, with smaller LLMs, where entity disambiguation has typically relied on reranking rather than reasoning. We ask when reasoning is worth its cost at small scale. We compare pointwise, listwise, and reasoning-based candidate-selection components within a classical coarse-to-fine entity disambiguation pipeline, across the classical, few-shot and true zero-shot settings. The reasoning paradigm is trained with distillation and reinforcement learning recipes. The benefit of reasoning grows with domain shift: negligible in-domain, decisive in the true zero-shot setting. We show that two distinct factors are at work: the reranker's uncertainty over the candidates locates where the paradigms disagree, while shift governs which is right when they do.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Entity Disambiguation (ED) is the task of mapping ambiguous mentions of entities in natural language text to reference entities in knowledge base (KB), each described by name and short description. For instance, in [Mercury] completes an orbit in 88 days, the mention Mercury must be resolved to the planet rather than to the chemical element or to the singer (Figure 1). Arrows give the mapping we find; labels give the training recipe for the reasoning paradigm. et al., 2022; De Cao et al., 2021; Haffoudhi et al., 2026a) and is an important preprocessing step for Information Extraction (Weikum et al., 2021), knowledge-based question answering (Li et al., 2020), knowledge graph completion (Ji and Grishman, 2011) and grounding language models in KBs (Crespin et al., 2026). ED can be performed in classical, few-shot, zero-shot, or true zero-shot setting, based on how close the training data is to the target (Haffoudhi et al., 2026b). Coarse-to-fine retrieve-and-rerank is the most widely adopted paradigm for ED (Wu et al., 2020): candidates are first retrieved, then scored against the context by reranker. Traditionally, these pipelines relied on BERT-based Pretrained Language Models (Wu et al., 2020), and recently, LLMs have pushed the ED state-of-the-art (Haffoudhi et al., 2026b; Zhou et al., 2024; Boscariol et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b; Ye and Mitchell, 2025). In particular, Reasoning LLMs enable true zero-shot entity linking (Haffoudhi et al., 2026b), generalizing across KBs and domains, by adding third reasoning-based LLM selection step, receiving as input the pointwise-rerankers top-k candidates. However, these results were obtained with large models, and the long chain-of-thoughtbased approaches induce substantial inference cost over the classical two-stage pipeline. Hence, it is unclear whether reasoning-based selection remains viable, or even beneficial, at small scales, and how those different paradigms compare in the other ED settings. Meanwhile, growing body of work studies how to elicit reasoning in language models through knowledge distillation and reinforcement learning (Guo et al., 2025; Muennighoff et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a), but whether such methods transfer to the ED task remains largely unexplored. Two questions follow: (1) given small LLM backbone, which selection paradigm pointwise reranking, direct listwise selection, or reasoning-based selection is best suited to each ED setting? (2) Can ED reasoning capabilities be transferred to small models, and which training paradigm knowledge distillation or reinforcement learning does so most effectively? To answer these questions, we conduct systematic study of small LLM backbones (0.64B) for ED across the classical, few-shot and true zero-shot3 settings (see Figure 1). First, we determine which candidate selection paradigm maximizes performance in each ED setting, and at what inference cost. Second, we find that the more uncertain the reranker is over its top-1 prediction, the more it is worth resorting to reasoning model. Finally, we show that domain shift matters because it drives that uncertainty up, and independently changes which candidate selection paradigm is right.

sections.title: 2.1 Entity Disambiguation
sections.content: ED is core component of Entity Linking together with mention detection (Sevgili et al., 2022; De Cao et al., 2021; Haffoudhi et al., 2026a). Classical supervised approaches are built on BERT-style encoders (Gillick et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2020), while generative methods decode entity identifiers autoregressively (De Cao et al., 2021). parallel line studies ED under progressively weaker supervision: the zero-shot setting, where test entities are unseen 3We omit plain zero-shot, as unseen test entities occur throughout, leaving domain shift as the only distinct challenge. but drawn from the training domain (Logeswaran et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2020), the few-shot setting, where only handful of targetdomain mentions are available (Li et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023b), and the true zeroshot setting, where neither entities nor domain are seen during training (Haffoudhi et al., 2026b). We adopt this taxonomy  (Table 1)  as the axis along which we compare candidate selection paradigms.

sections.title: 2.2 LLM-based Entity Disambiguation
sections.content: While retrieve-and-rerank dominate ED, LLMs have recently been applied to the candidate selection stage (Zhou et al., 2024; Ye and Mitchell, 2025; Shlyk et al., 2026), either scoring candidates pointwise, selecting from shortlist in listwise multiple-choice formulation, or, most recently, reasoning explicitly before selecting. In particular, Haffoudhi et al. (2026b) show that reasoningbased selection step enables true zero-shot ED. These gains, however, were obtained with large models and incur substantial inference cost. Li et al. (2025b) and concurrent work SelectED (Rücker et al., 2026) selectively invoke LLMs based on mention difficulty or confidence; our analysis characterizes when reasoning justifies its added cost.

sections.title: 2.3 Eliciting Reasoning in Small LLMs
sections.content: Two families of methods elicit reasoning in language models. Distillation (Hinton et al., 2015; Kim and Rush, 2016) transfers teachers behavior into student, either off-policy (Guo et al., 2025; Guha et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a) or onpolicy (Yang et al., 2025; Agarwal et al., 2023; Gu et al., 2023). Self-Distillation trains on-policy with the teacher being the student model with privileged information (Shenfeld et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), typically with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), instead optimizes reward function directly. Analyses of these paradigms suggest (1) that RLVR sharpens the sampling of solutions that the base model can already reach, while SFT introduces new capability (Yue et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025) and (2) that SFT memorizes while RLVR generalizes (Chu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Huan et al., 2026). While these methods are well studied on mathematical and coding reasoning (Li et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026), whether they transfer to ED, and how they compare across model scale and domain shift, remains unexplored. sections.title: 3.1 Task Definition and ED Settings
sections.content: Following Haffoudhi et al. (2026b), ED is defined using 4 random variables: (1) the domain (e.g. News, Biomedical etc), (2) the set of relevant entities E, (3) the text document , and (4) the set of mentions . It is posited that the set of relevant entities only depends on the domain D; the document only depends on the domain D; and the set of mentions only depends on the document and the set of entities E. The task of ED is that of linking the mentions in text document to their entities in E. We distinguish the following settings  (Table 1)  : In classical ED, one has access to documents sampled from distribution conditioned on the test entities and test domain. The few-shot setting shares the same structure as classical ED, but assumes that only mentions are observed during training. In zero-shot ED, the entities are distinct between train and test, but are sampled from the same domain. In the true zero-shot setting, none of the distributions are conditioned on the test domain. Pointwise reranking. Each candidate is scored independently by an LLM-based reranker (Zhang et al., 2025). We set the query to the context (with highlighted) and the document to the title and description of candidate e, and compute score(T, e) = σ(cid:0)ℓyes ℓno (cid:1), (1) where ℓyes, ℓno are the logits for yes/no relevance judgment and σ the logistic function. This stage requires nc forward passes per mention and sees every candidate, but scores them in isolation, without cross-candidate comparison. Direct selection. The top-k shortlist C(k) is passed to an instruction-tuned LLM in multiplechoice formulation: the prompt contains the context with highlighted and the candidates as an indexed list of (name, description) pairs. sections.title: 4.3 The True Zero-Shot Setting
sections.content: Benchmark. ZESHEL (Logeswaran et al., 2019) is benchmark for evaluating ED methods in zero-shot setting, built from Wikia9, Wikipedialike Web site for subjects such as fictional universes or sports. ZESHEL consists of 8 Wikia domains for training, 4 for validation, and 4 for testing. The test has total of 10,000 mentions. For each mention, the dataset provides 64 candidates retrieved by BM25. Entities correspond to Wikia pages, where the entity name is the title of the page and the entity description is its content. The candidate retrieval has recall of 68% on the test set. Configuration. Following previous work (Logeswaran et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022), we consider the normalized accuracy as the evaluation metric on ZESHEL, which is defined as the accuracy on the subset of mentions for which the correct entity is among the candidates. We use the provided candidates and the first three sentences of the entity page as the entity description. 9https://www.wikia.com/ Figure 3: Accuracy vs. base model size (left) and vs. inference FLOPs per linked mention (right, log scale), per setting. FLOPs exclude retrieval. Appendix D. Following Haffoudhi et al. (2026b), we consider = 10 for the reranking cutoff (see Appendix F) and sample = 10 completions per mention for majority voting and Pass@k metric computation (Appendix E). We set the maximum generation length to 2048 tokens and use the recommended generation parameters for each model. Each selection model is fed the shortlist of the largest reranker no bigger than itself, so that no paradigm benefits from larger upstream model. We also report results from prior methods. In particular, we include LELA (Haffoudhi et al., 2026b), the training-free LLM-based selector that our testtime-scaling paradigm builds on.

sections.title: 4.5 Analyses
sections.content: Uncertainty locates disagreement. Reranking and reasoning fail on much the same mentions, but which system is right when they disagree changes across settings  (Table 5)  . In the classical setting, reasoning breaks slightly more correct reranker predictions than it repairs; under true zero-shot shift, it repairs three times as many as it breaks. Writing z1 z2 for the log-odds gap between the rerankers top two candidates, disagreement falls steeply as this margin grows, while low-margin mentions become more frequent under shift (Figure 4a,c). sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We studied small LLM backbones for entity disambiguation, comparing candidate-selection paradigms and training recipes for reasoning-based selection across the classical, few-shot and true zero-shot settings. The resulting mapping is concrete: pointwise reranking suffices in the classical setting, where reasoning does not repay its inference cost; RLVR from distilled base is best given even hundred target-domain mentions; and offpolicy distillation performs best among the three main training recipes under pure domain shift, bringing 4B model within 1.2 points of its 26B teacher. ED reasoning is therefore not the preserve of large models. The mapping is not governed by the shift axis alone: reasoning pays where the reranker is uncertain over its candidates, and shift matters both because it drives that uncertainty up and because it decides which paradigm wins there. Our code is available on GitHub10 and our models on Hugging Face11.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Scale and model coverage. Our study spans 0.6 4B backbones from two model families (Qwen3 and Gemma-4), distilled from 2631B teachers. The recommendations we draw are specific to this range: we cannot say whether the paradigm ordering we observe holds for 8B+ students, different LLM-based rerankers, or whether it is stable across architectures we did not test. Nonetheless, our scale selection remains aligned with the typical sizes of rerankers, with larger model sizes being mostly limited to generative paradigms. Benchmarks and shift. We evaluate on English only, with domain shift instantiated by ZESHELs Wikia domains. While evaluation was conducted on four distinct domains, these are fictional universes with small, self-contained KBs, which is one particular kind of shift; whether our true zero-shot conclusions transfer to shifts of different character remains open. sections.title: 4.6 Discussion
sections.content: No single paradigm dominates, and the setting taxonomy alone does not say which one to use. Reranker uncertainty is second, partly independent axis: it locates the mentions where the paradigms diverge (examples in Appendix N), while the setting decides which of them is right there. That uncertainty has lexical counterpart in ZESHELs mention categories, and complements the established setting taxonomy and entityfrequency strata (De Cao et al., 2021) as an axis along which to compare ED systems. For training, off-policy distillation transfers better than RLVR under shift, whereas RLVR leads in few-shot adaptation by specializing to the target Coverage of the training design space. Our main comparison covers two GKD endpoints, supplemented by 22 ablation; intermediate settings remain unexplored. RLVR is represented by GRPO alone, and all runs use LoRA rather than full finetuning. Hyperparameters were held fixed across paradigms for comparability rather than tuned per paradigm, which may not favor each equally. Statistical scope. Each configuration corresponds to single training run, so variance across seeds and data orderings is not quantified. The claims we draw, however, are orderings that reproduce across three model sizes, two model families, and independent domains, rather than differences between individual runs; the per-domain results on ZESHEL, the results on GLADIS and the crossfamily replication each constitute an independent instantiation. Multi-seed replication of the full grid would multiply the training compute several-fold.

Results are reported in Table 14. At 4B, off-policy distillation improves over the reranker by 8.7 points on MC against 4.0 on LO and at most 1.2 elsewhere. MC is precisely the category in which every candidate shares the mentions surface form and differs only by disambiguation phrase, so lexical overlap carries no discriminative signal, making it the lexical counterpart of low reranker margin (Appendix J). sections.title: J Complementarity and Routing
sections.content: Setup. All of the following analyses compare Qwen3-Reranker-4B against the best reasoning variant at 4B in each setting, restricted to mentions whose gold entity is in the candidate shortlist. Margin-conditioned analyses additionally require at least two candidates, excluding 22.7% of ZELDA mentions. These excluded mentions contain no disagreements, so the margin-conditioned results use different denominator from Table 5. Metrics. Let denote the fraction of mentions on which the reranker is wrong and reasoning is correct, and the fraction on which the reranker is correct and reasoning is wrong. Their sum measures disagreement in correctness; it excludes mentions where both systems are wrong, even if their predictions differ. An oracle choosing the correct system whenever possible achieves the rerankers accuracy plus g. Table 16 supplements Table 5 with standalone and oracle accuracies, shared errors, and margin-based discrimination metrics. AUCcorr measures how well z1 z2 predicts reranker correctness; AUCroute measures how well it predicts that the reranker is correct among mentions where exactly one system is correct. Margin standardization. We use the margin bins shown in Figure 4. Let w(s) be the fraction of eligible mentions in setting falling in bin b, and d(s) the disagreement rate within that bin. The observed rate is d(s) = (cid:80) w(s) . Replacing each settings bin weights with the classical weights gives d(s) d(s) = (cid:88) d(s) wcls . (17) This compares settings under common margin distribution while preserving their within-bin disagreement rates. We apply the same weights separately to the within-bin repair and break rates, yielding g(s) and l(s), and report their ratio g(s)/l(s). This is the ratio of the standardized rates, not an average of within-bin ratios. The bin-level comparisons also reveal residual differences: true zero-shot disagreement is lower than classical disagreement in every bin above the lowest, whereas few-shot disagreement is higher in four of the six bins. Routing sweep. For each threshold, we use reasoning below the threshold and the rerankers prediction otherwise. We select separate threshold for each evaluation split, maximizing accuracy on that split itself. This gives an optimistic bound for this threshold-routing rule, rather than an estimate of deployable routers performance. The rule recovers 940% of the accuracy gap between the better standalone method and the oracle. In one of the four true-zero-shot domains, the optimal threshold routes every mention to reasoning, providing no inference saving over always using reasoning. Margin comparability. As diagnostic, we compare reranker top-1 accuracy within each bin with its classical value. The mass-weighted average deviation is 2.5 percentage points in few-shot and 4.0 in true zero-shot. The gap between them is the headroom left by plain self-consistency, and its behavior separates the paradigms sharply. Under RLVR, Maj@k is nearly flat even when Pass@k rises: additional samples contain correct answers, but majority voting rarely recovers them. sections.title: L Training Dynamics
sections.content: We study the training dynamics of the different paradigms under the three ED settings. To this end, we sample 250 random mentions from our ZELDA validation split and from each of the four ZESHEL test domains; and evaluate the different model checkpoints on those subsets throughout training. The learning curves are shown in Figure 10 for the classical and true zero-shot settings. Figure 11 shows the learning curve for the 4B models on the four domains. The evolution of Pass@1, Pass@10 and mean output tokens throughout training, in the classical and true zero-shot settings, are shown in Figure 12, and in Figure 13 in the fewshot domains. Non-reasoning paradigms. Reranking converges almost immediately and is flat thereafter: in the few-shot setting it reaches its final accuracy within the first hundred steps and stays there in all four domains (Figure 11). Direct selection is the opposite: it starts far below every other paradigm Figure 7: Accuracy vs. average output tokens per generation (log scale), per setting, for the TTS paradigms. and climbs throughout the run, at every scale (Figure 10), and remains the weakest curve in the few-shot domains. three Reasoning paradigms. The training recipes diverge in how their generations evolve. Under RLVR, trace length falls steadily while Pass@1 rises towards the base models Pass@10, consistent with the sampling-sharpening reading of Appendix K. Both distillation variants instead lengthen their traces as training proceeds. The on-policy variant at 2B degenerates, reaching (a) ZELDA (classical), 4B (b) ZESHEL (true zero-shot), 4B (c) ZELDA (classical), 2B (d) ZESHEL (true zero-shot), 2B (e) ZELDA (classical), 0.6B (f) ZESHEL (true zero-shot), 0.6B Figure 8: Pass@k and Maj@k over = 1, . . . , 10. Figure 9 gives the qualitative counterpart. Early in training all three paradigms produce the same task vocabulary (candidate, entity, context); by the late checkpoints the on-policy student is dominated by hedging and backtracking tokens, wait above all, whereas the RLVR students late traces retain the vocabulary of the task itself. The on-policy student is scored by teacher on its own trajectories, so drifting into ever longer deliberation is never directly penalised, whereas RLVRs binary reward, though itself indifferent to length, shortens traces as the policy concentrates. GRPO at 0.6B. At the smallest scale GRPO fails to train stably (Figure 10e,f): its curves remain erratic and below direct selection throughout, and the resulting model scores 48.25 on ZESHEL  (Table 3)  . This is consistent with RLVR requiring the base model to reach correct completions often enough for the pass-band filter of Section 3.4 to yield usable signal. Few-shot adaptation. Adaptation converges quickly for every paradigm, but not at the same rate: reranking is flat from the first checkpoints, 12A preliminary rerun using full-vocabulary distillation showed improved training stability. whereas the reasoning recipes take several hundred steps to reach their final accuracy (Figure 11). Forgetting under Domain-Adaptation Table 17 reports accuracy on ZELDA/AIDA after few-shot adaptation to each ZESHEL domain, against the same checkpoint before adaptation. Every paradigm loses some source-domain accuracy, but not to the same degree: RLVR loses between 2.0 and 5.8 points depending on the target domain, whereas both distillation variants stay within 1.4 in every case, and are statistically indistinguishable from the unadapted checkpoint in three out of the four domains. The pointwise reranker and direct selection sit in between.
